item.title: How Small Mistakes Might Sometimes Exhibit Good Thinking
item.description:
Decision-Making

How Small Mistakes Might Sometimes Exhibit Good Thinking

Thinking about losing gravity and Project Anchor.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Balancing skepticism and open-mindedness is a key to sound critical thinking.
  • It’s not irrational to act on extremely unlikely events when the cost of caution is low.
  • Science accepts its own limitations and values skepticism.

Open-mindedness is an important aspect of critical thinking, as the latter requires the consideration of multiple perspectives; however, it’s also important to be sceptical, particularly in situations where the evidence for a perspective is lacking (Dwyer et al., 2016). With respect to balance, the context of the situation should help guide how you engage these dispositions.

The Viral Conspiracy Theory of 7 Seconds Without Gravity

Almost a year ago, I started seeing rumours online that we would "lose gravity" for seven seconds at 2:33 p.m. GMT on August 12. Postulations suggested numerous potential causes, including black hole, eclipse, and experimentation activities. But, as most of these warnings suggested that "NASA knows about it," it was also a conspiracy belief.

Of course, I was extremely sceptical. I set an alarm for it months in advance, not because I believed it, but because I wanted to be present-minded for the nonsense to be debunked. I wanted a laugh to myself at 2:33 p.m. on that day. I knew (because I did physics in school) that in light of the moon’s orbit around us and the sun’s pull on Earth, for gravity to cease, you’d pretty much need to stop the planet and everything on it from having mass—meaning I also knew that this was close to impossible. So, why then, on that day two weeks ago, at 2:32 p.m., did I actually consider organising my family at our staircase to hold on to the balusters for a few moments?

The "Just in Case" Principle

Why do you buy insurance? Just in case. Indeed, despite the lack of evidence to support this prediction, I was open-minded enough to concern myself with a what-if scenario, if for nothing more than an exercise in caution, in which case I would consider the potential for it happening and the weight of the outcome relative to the cost to me of being cautious. That is, we’d only lose a minute or two of our lives, and I’d just look silly in front of my wife. (My kids are too young to understand what we’d be doing.) The mistake would not be costly. However, if the 0.00000000001 percent chance of this conspiracy belief being right came to fruition, at least we’d be prepared to avoid potential serious injury when gravity returned.

As we moved closer to the date, one of my favourite examples from teaching classes on epistemology and the nature of "proof" kept coming to mind. We can’t prove anything. Gravity is a theory. Take this pen for example. I know that when I release it from my hand, it will accelerate to the ground at 9.81 m/s2. I’d bet my house on it. What goes up must come down. We have observed this time and time again, without it being disproved (hence why it is a theory). But that doesn’t mean that one day, some massive asteroid can’t hit Earth and somehow knock us off our axis, thus potentially messing up our gravity. That’s why science is cautious. We cannot see into the future. We cannot prove, only disprove.

article continues after advertisement

With that, what if, as with some other conspiracy beliefs, certain points are partially true (Dwyer, 2025)? For example, what if we lost gravity or some other major disaster occurred at that time? It wouldn’t have to be because of the silly examples the conspiracy theorists suggested, which were rather easily debunked, but because of something else. Practically, who cares about the what or why in this scenario, when it’s the outcome that really matters?

Open-Nindedness Versus Skepticism

I don’t know everything. Science doesn’t know everything. The public doesn’t know everything. At 2:32 that day, the open-minded part of me suggested that maybe we could lose gravity for a reason that not a single person on Earth has ever considered before, and the one thing that was right was the date and time. Whereas the sceptic said, "Without any credible evidence, the same can be said about any date/time…"

In my previous example, I said "betting my house on it" that gravity will work in terms of releasing the pen. That bet was still on back on August 12, because I certainly didn’t increase my house insurance in advance. Had I somewhere to be, I wouldn’t have thought twice about being out in the open air. But, as things turned out, I was at home. At 2:32, I got up from my desk in the office and went into the kitchen to be with my family to "make some coffee"... not because I believed something would happen (I didn’t); rather, because of caution. I’m not going to risk the safety of my family, no matter how small the odds, because of my pride (be it in science, scepticism, source credibility, etc.), when the cost of open-minded caution was so little. Again, caution, not belief.

Yes, I’m prideful of science. But I also understand its strengths and "limitations." Unfortunately, many people often get the notion of science wrong. Perhaps that’s a reason why there has been increased distrust in it over the past decade. (See my previous post on the "post-truth era.")

For example, a common complaint I hear from religious individuals, in an attempt to justify their faith, is that science arrogantly believes it knows everything. That’s not the case. Scientists do not think they know everything, because, as Irish comedian Dara Ó Briain once correctly joked, if they did, then science would just stop (i.e., what’s the point of "sciencing" if we already know everything?). Scientists recognise and celebrate the many knowledge gaps that require filling. That’s what makes science exciting—the opportunity for discovering and learning new things, as well as advancing what we thought we already knew (e.g., again, disproving versus proving).

We all get things wrong sometimes. Even the best thinkers, from time to time, make a decision based on their gut alone and get it horribly wrong. When science gets something wrong, it’s often because new, innovative research has facilitated us in learning more about the topic and adds to our knowledge base, thus "changing" it. Being wrong affords us new and better understanding. That’s a good thing. We can learn from being wrong, in which case, the big mistake of being wrong would be not learning from it.

article continues after advertisement

Good Thinking Requires Both Caution and Critical Judgement

A big mistake, personally, would have been me actually changing my insurance policy in light of this conspiracy belief. Of course, though, good thinking stops me from doing that, knowing I had no credible evidence to support the possibility of this event occurring (i.e., scepticism). I wasn’t wrong about it, because I didn’t believe it; but I did make "a mistake" out of caution (i.e., open-mindedness), in that I cost myself a minute or two of my life. But, at least I had a fresh cup of coffee out of it. It was a mistake I was happy to make…just in case.

Good thinking isn’t about being wrong or right; it’s about, as best possible, ensuring good decision-making, and caution is core to good decision-making.

item.title: Why Grief Has a Geography
item.description:
Grief

Why Grief Has a Geography

The psychology of distant disasters, and the awareness we can train.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Grief and empathy weaken with distance, a phenomenon shaped by evolutionary social wiring.
  • Compassion can be expanded through practices like loving-kindness and mindful awareness.
  • The reach of empathy is not fixed; psychological research shows it grows with effort.

This week, flash floods swept through Nepal. Thousands of lives were lost overnight. Families shattered. Villages erased.

If you felt a moment of sorrow reading that sentence and then felt the sorrow fade as your attention returned to your day, you have just experienced one of the most consistent and unsettling findings in the psychology of empathy: Our grief has a geography. It travels along the lines of our identities and thins with distance.

The Psychology of Distant Loss

Psychologists have documented this pattern for decades. We respond powerfully to a single identified life in danger and far less to thousands of statistical lives, a phenomenon researchers call the identifiable victim effect. As numbers grow, feeling shrinks, a collapse of compassion sometimes described as psychic numbing. Our empathy is also strongly modulated by group membership. Lives that share our community, our language, our nationality, or our alma mater register more deeply than lives that do not.

None of this makes us bad people. These are ancient features of a social brain that evolved in small groups, where the suffering that mattered for survival was the suffering nearby. But in a world where we witness planetary loss daily, on our phones, in real time, these features leave us strangely calibrated: flooded with information about distant suffering and equipped with hearts that reach only so far.

A question worth asking is whether the reach of the heart is fixed or if it can be trained.

An Old Answer: Expand the Circle

Contemplative traditions worldwide arrived at a shared answer long before psychology existed as a field. The Buddhist practice of loving-kindness deliberately extends care outward in widening circles, from oneself to loved ones, to strangers, to all beings. In the yogic traditions of India, masters like Sadhguru speak of cultivating a mother's heart for the world, a state in which every life registers the way the lives closest to us do, not because of proximity or shared identity, but simply because a life is a life.

I have received this teaching in my own contemplative journey, and I will be honest: I do not know whether I have truly expanded to it. Most of us have not. But the traditions treat this capacity the way an athlete treats strength: something built through daily practice. And that claim, unlike many spiritual claims, is now testable.

A More Personal Question

Reflecting on Nepal, I found myself asking a harder question: What would I do if I faced such a disaster myself? No time to react. No escape. The only answer that came to me was this: Be fully aware, simply present to whatever is happening, including the end.

A preparation for that exists, taught for centuries and available to anyone. "Each night before sleep, rest your attention on the breath", says Sadhguru. Watch it, without controlling it, until sleep arrives. What falls asleep is the body and the mind. What remains, awareness itself, may be the most permanent thing about us.

article continues after advertisement

Knowing this is very different from living it.

What the Research Shows

Awareness is not only a contemplative idea. It is a measurable psychological capacity, and studies from our research group on Inner Engineering suggest it responds to training across every timescale examined.

  • Within weeks: In a published six-week study of a breath-based meditation practice, Shambhavi, participants showed significant gains in mindful attention and awareness on the validated Mindful Attention Awareness Scale, alongside a 41 percent reduction in perceived stress and a 50 percent reduction in negative emotions, with improved sleep quality (Frontiers in Psychology, 2022). A companion study of a related guided meditation found anxiety reduced by 36 percent and depressive symptoms by 46 percent over the same period (Frontiers in Psychiatry, 2022).
  • Over a year: In a 12-month follow-up study, these gains did not fade once the novelty wore off. Stress reductions, well-being gains, and mindful awareness deepened with continued practice (Frontiers in Psychology, 2025).
  • Over a lifetime: Long-term meditators show a biological brain age nearly six years younger than matched controls, and electroencephalography reveals greater meta-awareness, less mind wandering, and deeper meditative states (Mindfulness, 2025 and 2026). Preliminary data from a large study currently under peer review on a seven-minute free meditation practice, Miracle of Mind, suggest that even a single brief guided session can shift emotional state, with the largest changes in those who begin with the lowest well-being.

The pattern across these studies is consistent. The capacity for awareness, the very capacity the traditions say can widen the reach of the heart, strengthens with practice the way a muscle strengthens with use.

Better to Be Prepared

My deepest hope is that no one reading this ever faces what the people of Nepal faced this week. But life does not consult us. And when the unthinkable arrives, whatever remains to us will be whatever we have practiced. The nightly return to the breath costs nothing, requires no belief, and appears to be quietly building something in us, week by week, year by year.

Perhaps it builds something else, too: a heart whose grief travels a little farther than its geography.

My heart goes out to every life lost and affected in Nepal.

item.title: What 5 Breakup Movies Teach Us About Moving On
item.description:
Relationships

What 5 Breakup Movies Teach Us About Moving On

From rumination to resilience, five films for wherever you are in grief.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • A 2026 study found no single path through heartbreak, but three distinct recovery patterns.
  • Film can externalize grief, offering perspective that “loss-focused” rumination lacks.
  • Most young adults report their breakup became a positive turning point, not just a loss.
  • Research shows many people regain a sense of freedom and energy within three months of a breakup.
Meme of "Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind"
Source: Focus Features

Ending a long-term relationship is one of the most stressful life events we go through. The movie Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004) seems to have more Internet memes than people who saw it in theaters, because the film precisely captures the dread of heartbreak, loss, and longing.

The story goes something like this: A whimsical twentysomething, Clementine (Kate Winslet), undergoes a procedure to erase her memories of her former boyfriend Joel (Jim Carrey) to avoid the pain of ending the relationship. When Joel discovers that Clementine has forgotten him, he undergoes the same procedure so he is not left suffering, but soon realizes that those memories are worth keeping. Even as he tries to hide Clementine in the deepest corners of his mind, the software completes its job, and he forgets.

The premise is that if we could just have a computer erase our memories, we would avoid the pain of loss and heartbreak, but we would also lose the beautiful memories and moments that make us who we are. Pain can build resilience, and we can grow and learn to thrive through our hardships. Loss is part of our human development. While it is painful and difficult to lose someone you once loved, most young adults view breaking up as a positive turning point in their lives. Research has shown that we can and do recover from breakups within three months, feeling a greater sense of freedom and renewed energy.

In a 2026 study published in the Journal of Loss & Trauma, researchers found there is no direct route to recovering from a breakup, but there are many ways we can find our way back from heartbreak. One of the most common ways they found was a "Pain to Relief, Reflection, and Growth" model, in which individuals experience initial distress, followed by reflection that produces insights. Another path they identified was the “Resilient and Moving On” model, where individuals radically accept the loss and take proactive steps to let go and move on with less reflection. The third path they looked at was the “Loss-Focused and Continuous Grief” model, which was the most difficult and led to the most rumination and distress.

Below, I am recommending another "model" to deal with heartbreak—the "Emotional Release, Healthy Distraction, and New Perspective" Model—or, as I like to call it, reel therapy.

Five films to help you get through a breakup

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind (2004): In this film, we grieve with Joel (Jim Carrey) as he painfully learns the ache of heartbreak through the loss of beautiful memories from a relationship that has abruptly ended.

article continues after advertisement
"500 Days of Summer"
Source: Fox Searchlight Pictures

500 Days of Summer (2009): Tom (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) believes he has found "the One" and builds an entire narrative to convince himself, only to realize he was projecting his desires rather than seeing reality.

"Sliding Doors"
Source: Miramax

Sliding Doors (1998): This movie is a little gem that lets Helen (Gwyneth Paltrow) play out the what-if scenario (via sliding doors), underscoring how unfair loss can feel and that growth is not guaranteed by circumstance.

"Forgetting Sarah Marshall"
Source: Focus Features

Forgetting Sarah Marshall (2008): This film is cathartic because it has you crying-laughing the entire time. Peter (Jason Segel) realizes he and his ex changed and that it was not about being "wronged" by her but about understanding they want different things.

"Past Lives"
Source: A24

Past Lives (2023): This bittersweet film grieves what young love could have become, but also shows us gratitude for what Nora (Greta Lee) actually has in her current relationship and life.

item.title: How Sport Psychology Helps C-Suite Women Perform Their Best
item.description:
Career

How Sport Psychology Helps C-Suite Women Perform Their Best

Three key shifts from sport psychology that help women enhance work performance.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Concepts from sport psychology can help C-suite women build sustainable performance.
  • Skills like mindfulness, attentional focus, and physical resets are not just for athletes.
  • Sport psychology can help executive women lead with more clarity under pressure.
Source: Christina/Wocintechchat/Unsplash

Many people believe sport psychology is only for elite athletes. The truth is, we are all performers. We all perform in something every day, whether it’s sport, work, tests, parenting, presentations, or leadership. All of these areas require a certain mindset and deliberate behaviors to excel.

Sport psychology can be particularly powerful for C-suite women. As a female executive navigating quarterly planning, budget decisions, board meetings, client pitches, and high-visibility strategy, you need tools that match the demand. Sport psychology can offer a useful lens to help you with thoughts, habits, and stress responses that impact how you lead and show up at work, especially under pressure. Here are three meaningful shifts that C-suite women can incorporate into their work to facilitate more sustainable performance.

Shift 1: Recognize when pressure starts running the show

One of the first skills I teach clients in therapy is mindfulness. Mindfulness allows us to identify and understand thoughts, feelings, and other internal experiences. For many C-suite women, it’s easy for burnout to sneak up on you without you realizing it. That’s why an awareness of what’s happening inside our bodies and minds is so important.

For many clients, the pressure itself isn’t the problem. Many leaders enjoy challenge, responsibility, and meaningful goals. The problem is how we relate to that pressure, whether we view stress as a challenge or opportunity instead of a threat.

Here are some signs that you might be operating from fear of failure (avoidance strategy), rather than a drive towards success (approach strategy).

  1. Over-functioning: You feel like you have to be the one to do it all. You feel like no one else can do your job the way you can. You avoid taking vacation or rest days, even when you’re sick or exhausted. You check email constantly. You have trouble delegating and often jump in to solve challenges before your team has a chance to.
  2. Unforgiving inner critic: Nothing ever feels good enough. You reach towards a goal for months, and after achieving it, you feel “meh.” After you finish a task or big project, you go right into the next one without acknowledging your effort. When others give you compliments, you brush them off.
  3. Rigid perfectionism: You have perfectionistic behaviors that are hard to turn off. You have high expectations for yourself and others that don’t adjust based on changing circumstances. You prepare way more than a meeting requires to avoid being caught off guard. You find yourself replaying conversations and pitches over and over to “check” that you did a good job. You agonize over decisions, exhausting all the pros and cons to make sure it's the “right” one.
article continues after advertisement

The first step towards making a change is recognizing what is actually happening. If you see yourself in these signs, it might be time to consider how you are relating to the pressure of work and if sport psychology could be beneficial. Sport psychology can be a helpful resource to support values-consistent behaviors, sustainable leadership, and overall well-being.

Shift 2: Direct your attention with intention

One of the ways pressure can sneak up on us is by grabbing our attentional resources. It’s easy to get sucked into the next fire that needs to be put out, or worrying about all possible negative outcomes, rather than being intentional about where you are spending your time and energy.

C-suite women have many competing attentional demands, at work and at home. In therapy, we use mindfulness and attentional control skills to help direct your focus where you want it to be. During a difficult meeting, that may mean coming back to the decision in front of you rather than trying to read every mind in the room or predict every possible outcome.

When your mind starts racing ahead, it can help to have a simple way to refocus before a major presentation, negotiation, or difficult conversation. You might try:

  • Set one clear intention: Define your primary focus for the interaction before stepping into the room. Focus on short cue words that you can remember.

  • Extend your exhalations: Slow your breathing prior to the pressure situation. Lengthening your exhale helps your nervous system calm down from fight-or-flight mode.

  • Control what’s controllable: Identify and commit to a single action that’s entirely within your control. Try to avoid taking responsibility for outcomes outside of your control.

article continues after advertisement

The goal isn’t to eliminate nerves or self-doubt before you lead. The goal is to notice those feelings without letting them pull you away from what matters in the moment. With practice, you can get better at returning to the conversation, decision, or task in front of you. That doesn’t mean never feeling distracted or uncertain, but facing high-pressure situations with intention, rather than reaction.

Shift 3: Recover more intentionally between high-stakes moments

Many high-achieving women have been conditioned to push through exhaustion in difficult moments. When you’ve been doing that for a long time, slowing down can feel much harder.

Successful people know that recovery time is essential. But knowing this and actually building it in are two different things. However, recovery is not a luxury earned only when the workday ends. It’s an active performance strategy to protect your bandwidth, and an essential performance metric. Framing it in this way can help you step away without guilt, even in busy work seasons.

Here are three practical strategies for C-suite women to recover more intentionally.

  • A three-minute buffer: Schedule a non-negotiable pause between back-to-back calendar holds/meetings to step away from screens. This allows your brain to download all the previous information and reset before taking in new information.
  • Physical de-escalation: After a stressful meeting or mental shift, use a physical reset to signal to your body that you can close the book on the previous task. Dig your feet into the ground, noting the sensations at each touch point of your foot: your heel, your toes, your arch, and the ball of your foot. Take three centering breaths, focusing on long exhales (I like paced breathing, breathing in for a count of four, and breathing out for a count of six).
  • An anchor for end-of-day: Establish a deliberate end-of-day ritual, like closing all browser tabs, shutting down your laptop, or turning off the light at your desk. Take a moment to then visualize yourself putting the day aside. Visualize putting your worries or tasks in a box that will be there for you tomorrow.

It’s easy to get stuck in all-or-nothing thinking, believing that recovery is impactful only if it’s “big” (think full-day retreats, a spa day, or an extended vacation). Those things can all be beneficial, but remember that small recovery shifts can be more impactful than you think.

Build a more sustainable version of high performance

article continues after advertisement

C-suite women are often expected to be the calmest person in the room while carrying an enormous amount of responsibility. You don’t need to become tougher or more productive. Sustainable performance means understanding how pressure affects you and learning how to keep showing up in a way that feels aligned with your values.

Highly capable women absolutely benefit from a space where they don’t have to be “on,” but can just be themselves in a highly supportive environment. Individual therapy provides a highly confidential space where the expectation to perform is completely removed. Therapy can help you make room for your goals and for yourself. It can help to look honestly at what’s working, what feels exhausting, and what needs to shift, all while having someone in your corner to help encourage you.

To find a therapist, please visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: AI and the Brand You Didn't Build
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

AI and the Brand You Didn't Build

AI is changing how the identities we build are understood.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • AI is creating an inferred brand beyond the brand we deliberately express.
  • The inference gap is the distance between those two identities.
  • The INFER framework helps us understand and manage what AI concludes about us.
Source: Maria Maltseva/Pixabay

We all have an individual brand. Our clothes, words, and ideas all project signals about who we are or who we want to be.

I've spent more than 25 years building brands, including senior roles at Ogilvy, where much of my work involved a deceptively simple yet critical question: How do you shape what people think about a company, brand, or individual? Of course, what a brand intends to communicate and what people actually perceive have never been exactly the same. That gap is as old as branding itself and has often kept me up at night.

But AI is changing the calculus because the interpreter is changing.

From Expression to Inference

Traditional branding is largely overt, and that's by design. Companies choose hallmarks that include things like names, logos, colors, typography, imagery, and messages. These are often crafted with extraordinary attention and enormous budgets. The best brands can go deeper and create emotional connections that can make a swoosh or an apple carry meaning far beyond color and typography. It's the formation of a relationship between the user and the brand.

AI encounters a brand very differently. Large language models can draw upon corporate websites, journalism, reviews, research, social commentary, historical references, and just about any online information. Some of those signals are carefully created by the organization, while many are not. AI gathers this material and constructs something like a probabilistic portrait that can be far from the "brand persona" that a company or person intends.

This creates what I think of as two versions of a brand. There is the expressed brand, the identity we deliberately create and communicate based on traditional brand hallmarks, and increasingly there is the inferred brand. That's the identity AI reconstructs from the signals, intended or unintended, surrounding us. The interesting question, for me and most marketers, is how closely those two portraits match.

Being Found Isn't Being Understood

Business has long used frameworks such as SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats) and PEST (political, economic, social, and technological) to understand an organization and the world around it. The digital era brought SEO (search engine optimization), and now GEO (generative engine optimization) asks whether AI and LLMs can find and surface a person or organization. These tools answer useful questions, but being found is not the same as being understood. None of them quite capture the identity AI constructs once it has gathered the available signals.

article continues after advertisement

Think about a physician who has spent 20 years building a reputation around a particular clinical area. Her website reflects it, her colleagues know it, and patients may seek her out specifically because of it. Yet ask a few LLMs about her and another portrait might emerge. Perhaps an older affiliation or even a resolved malpractice claim from the past dominates the answer. Her research is barely mentioned, or she is described in the same generic language used for dozens of physicians in the field. And the same applies to large corporations where issues outside the conventions of branding drive AI output.

Nothing necessarily has to be factually wrong for the portrait to be wrong. The problem can simply be the distance between the identity she has spent years building and the identity AI has inferred from the available evidence. Once that inferred version begins circulating first, the expressed self can find itself arguing with a portrait that never truly existed.

That raises a new question for individuals and organizations alike: What does AI infer about you?

A Framework for Inference

Leveraging my brand-building work in the past, I've been thinking about that question through a framework I call INFER. It offers five ways to examine the identity that emerges when AI interprets the signals surrounding a person, company, or organization.

  • I—Identity. Look at the portrait itself. What does AI think you are?
  • N—Narrative. Look across different questions and contexts. What story keeps emerging, and what gets left out?
  • F—Fidelity. Compare that portrait with the identity you intended to create. How close are they?
  • E—Evidence. Where did this version of you come from? The sources and signals shaping the inference may be very different from the ones you expected.
  • R—Resilience. Change the model, change the question, or come back six months later. Is the identity still recognizably you?

INFER isn't intended to replace SWOT, PEST, or the traditional tools of branding. It examines something those frameworks were never designed to see, and that's the distance between the identity we express and the identity machines infer. That's the inference gap, and it's critical to a business or an individual.

article continues after advertisement

When AI Becomes the Interpreter

AI is a curious if not quirky kind of audience. It doesn't buy your product or walk into your store. It interprets you for people who might. Someone can ask an LLM which company is most innovative in an industry, which university has the strongest academics, which physician is known for a procedure, or which car mechanic is better. Increasingly, the response arrives as a coherent answer rather than a page of links that requires the person to do the interpreting.

This reaches well beyond corporations. Universities, hospitals, nonprofits, executives, scientists, physicians, authors, and perhaps all of us increasingly have identities that can be reconstructed by AI. The accumulated record of "us" becomes part of the informational corpus from which those telling inferences are made.

For years, we have thought carefully about the brands we present to the world, from the colors and symbols we choose to the messaging we hope will define us. AI adds another layer because our identity is increasingly being encountered by machines that gather those signals and construct a version of us that others may encounter first.

Branding has always been about crafting a meaning, real or perceived. And AI is becoming a participant in how that meaning is conjured and formed. As that role grows, understanding the brand we deliberately express may no longer be enough. We also need to understand the brand that AI infers, where that inference comes from, and how closely it resembles the identity we thought we were putting into the world.

item.title: Your Insurance Says 70 Percent, but You Got Only $140 Back
item.description:
Therapy

Your Insurance Says 70 Percent, but You Got Only $140 Back

Reimbursement runs on a number your insurer picks and rarely explains.

Posted August 29, 2026

Key points
  • Insurers reimburse a percentage of their own "allowed amount," often far below big-city mental health fees.
  • Out-of-network deductibles are separate from in-network deductibles, and typically higher.
  • Under the No Surprises Act, you're entitled to a written Good Faith Estimate before scheduled care.
  • A few plans, including some New York State employee plans, carry unusually strong out-of-network benefits.

A patient pays $500 for a psychiatric visit. Her plan documents say it covers 70 percent of out-of-network care. The reimbursement check arrives for $140.

That check is correct. The plan worked exactly as designed. I'm a psychiatrist, and I walk patients through this arithmetic often enough that I think the design deserves a plain-language explanation, because the gap between what people expect back and what they receive is one of the most common sources of frustration in private mental health care. It's better understood before your first appointment than after your first claim.

The Number You Never See

When a plan says it covers 70 percent of out-of-network care, most people reasonably read that as: I pay $500, I get $350 back.

Insurers don't reimburse a percentage of what you were charged. They reimburse a percentage of what they've internally decided the service should cost. That figure goes by several names, including the allowed amount, UCR (usual, customary and reasonable), or MRC (maximum reimbursable charge). The insurer sets it, often by benchmarking to a multiple of Medicare rates, and in expensive markets it frequently sits far below what clinicians actually charge.

A comparison from ordinary working life makes the structure familiar. Suppose your employer reimburses 70 percent of business travel, but caps hotels at $150 a night no matter what the hotel charged. Book a $400 room, and you get back $105, an effective rate of 26 percent. The 70 percent was real. It just applied to a number your employer chose, in a document you probably never read.

Health insurance works the same way. Here's the actual arithmetic on that $500 visit:

  • Charged fee: $500
  • Insurer's allowed amount: $200 (the insurer decides this)
  • Coverage rate: 70 percent
  • Reimbursement: $140
  • Your out-of-pocket: $360

In other words, the advertised 70 percent became an effective 28 percent. Nobody misled you in a way you could point to. The percentage and the fee were both accurate. They were just percentages of different numbers.

I want to be fair to both sides here. This isn't a clinician billing anyone unfairly, and it isn't exactly an insurer breaking a promise. It's a gap between what care costs in a given market and what a plan has decided to recognize. But patients who did the math the intuitive way feel misled, and I understand why.

The Second Deductible

There's a second mechanism stacked on the first. Nearly all commercial plans maintain two separate deductibles: one for in-network care and a second, typically higher one, for out-of-network care. Money paid toward one doesn't count toward the other.

Out-of-network deductibles commonly run $1,000 to $5,000 for an individual. Until that deductible is met, nothing comes back at all. And it accrues at the allowed amount, which is the punchline most people miss: If your out-of-network deductible is $3,000 and the allowed amount is $200 per visit, it takes 15 visits before the first reimbursement check arrives.

The Paperwork That Gets Your Money Back

Out-of-network clinicians don't bill your insurer. You pay directly, and the practice gives you a superbill, an itemized statement listing the dates of service, the procedure and diagnosis codes, and the clinician's identifiers. You submit it to your insurer, usually through a member portal, and reimbursement comes to you.

It's mundane, and it matters. Patients leave real money unclaimed every year because nobody explained that the superbill isn't a receipt to file away. It's a claim form waiting to be submitted.

What You're Entitled to Before You Book

Under the federal No Surprises Act, in effect since January 2022, providers must give uninsured and self-pay patients a written Good Faith Estimate of expected charges before scheduled care. You can request one from any practice. If the final bill exceeds the estimate by $400 or more, a formal dispute process exists.

article continues after advertisement

Ask for it. A practice that can't produce a written estimate of what your care will cost is telling you something.

The Plans That Surprise in the Other Direction

Everything above describes the typical case. There's a less-known flip side worth checking. A minority of plans carry out-of-network mental health benefits that are genuinely strong, with allowed amounts close to actual market fees. Several New York State employee plans are known for this, and people holding them often have no idea. I've seen patients assume private care was out of reach when their plan would have reimbursed most of it.

One phone call settles it. Ask your insurer three things:

  • What is the allowed amount for an initial psychiatric evaluation and a follow-up visit?
  • What is my out-of-network deductible, and how much of it have I met?
  • What percentage applies after the deductible?

With those three answers, you can compute your real cost per visit before you ever book.

The broader point holds anywhere in the country: The percentage on your insurance card is the least informative number in the equation. The allowed amount is the one that determines what you'll actually pay, and you're allowed to ask for it.
